summary: Describes how GMPLS Label Switched Paths can be aggregated into a hierarchy to improve scalability. A router can create a TE path and advertise it as a forwarding adjacency, a link that other paths can use. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Many small roads can merge into one highway, and cars drive the highway as if it were just another road. This memo explains that layered trick for network paths.

questions: what is lsp hierarchy in gmpls
subtitle: How a GMPLS router can turn a traffic-engineered path into a link that other paths nest inside.

tldr.problem: GMPLS networks can have many LSPs, and aggregating them into a hierarchy would improve scalability, but a way is needed to create and use such aggregates.
tldr.mechanism: A router creates a TE LSP, advertises it into the same ISIS/OSPF instance as a TE link called a forwarding adjacency (FA), lets other routers use the FA in path computation, and nests their LSPs inside it using the label stack.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4206 defines the routing parameters, signalling procedures for RSVP-TE and CR-LDP, LSP region boundaries and holding priority rules for this. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 6107.

sections.title: Overview of Forwarding Adjacencies
sections.content:
A Label Switching Router (LSR) uses GMPLS traffic engineering procedures to create an LSP. Under local configuration control, it may then announce that LSP as a Traffic Engineering (TE) link into the same instance of the GMPLS control plane (its ISIS/OSPF part) that was used to create it. Such a link is a forwarding adjacency (FA), and the LSP is the FA-LSP. The concept applies only when one control plane instance both creates the LSP and uses it as a TE link.

The nodes at the ends of a basic TE link may have a routing adjacency, but the nodes joined by an FA would not usually have one. Any TE link still needs a signaling adjacency before an LSP can be set up across it.

ISIS/OSPF floods FAs like any other link, so each LSR's TE link state database holds both basic TE links and FAs. When computing a path, an LSR uses both, and then uses RSVP or CR-LDP to establish label bindings along it. Creating or tearing down an FA can be driven by configuration outside GMPLS or by LSP setup requests that arrive from other LSRs.

Out of scope are advertising an LSP as a plain point-to-point link for use by nodes other than the head-end, and cases where one control plane instance creates the LSP and another instance uses it as a link.
sections.plainLanguage: A router builds a private tunnel and then tells everyone, there is a new road here. Other routers can then plan trips along that road, and many trips can ride inside the tunnel together.

sections.title: Advertising an FA in Routing
sections.content:
An FA may be numbered or unnumbered. If it is numbered with IPv4 addresses, the local and remote addresses come from a /31 allocated by the LSR that originates the FA-LSP. The head-end address is the IPv4 tunnel sender address, and the tail-end address can be inferred from it.

If several LSPs run between the same two LSRs, they could be merged into one FA using link bundling, or each could be advertised as its own adjacency.

When an FA is created by static provisioning, its attributes come from configuration: the head-end address (default: the head-end LSR's Router ID), the tail-end address, and bandwidth and resource color constraints. The path is either computed by the head-end or explicitly configured. When an FA is created dynamically, it inherits the attributes of the LSP that triggered it. Its bandwidth must be at least that of the triggering LSP, and may be larger when only discrete bandwidths are available. The RFC notes a policy mechanism may be needed to assign attributes to dynamic FA-LSPs.

Two further points: FAs are not expected to be used to establish ISIS/OSPF peering between the routers at their ends. To restrict an FA to TE path computation only, IS-IS can set the default metric of the extended IS reachability TLV to the maximum link metric (2^24 - 1), and OSPF can advertise it only as a TE opaque LSA and not as a regular LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: When the new tunnel-road is announced, the announcement says where it starts, where it ends and how much traffic it can hold. If you are building it ahead of time you write those details yourself, and if it was built because someone needed it, it copies the details of the trip that caused it.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering Parameters of an FA
sections.content:
The RFC fixes how each TE parameter in the OSPF and IS-IS TE extensions is filled in for an FA. In OSPF the Link Type is point-to-point and the Link ID is the Router ID of the FA-LSP tail-end. For a numbered FA, the local interface address is the head-end address and the remote address is the tail-end address. Unnumbered FAs follow the unnumbered-link signalling RFCs.

By default the TE metric is max(1, (the TE metric of the FA-LSP path) - 1), so that the FA attracts traffic in preference to setting up a new LSP. Maximum Reservable Bandwidth and the initial Maximum LSP Bandwidth default to the bandwidth of the FA-LSP, and the initial unreserved bandwidth is also the FA-LSP bandwidth. By default an FA has no resource colors. All of these can be overridden by configuration at the head-end.

The near-end Interface Switching Capability of the FA is that of the first link in the FA-LSP. For PSC-1 to PSC-4, the Interface MTU is the minimum MTU along the FA-LSP path and the Minimum LSP Bandwidth is the bandwidth of the LSP.

An FA advertisement may also carry Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) information: the union of the SRLGs of the underlying TE links on the FA-LSP path. If FAs are bundled and the bundle carries an SRLG TLV, the SRLG lists must be the same for each component FA-LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new tunnel-road gets a price tag, a size limit and a type. By default the price is set slightly below the real cost, so drivers prefer the tunnel to digging a new one.

sections.title: LSP Regions and FA-LSP Boundaries
sections.content:
To control where FA-LSPs begin and end, the RFC introduces the LSP region, built from Interface Switching Capabilities. Capabilities are ordered PSC-1 < PSC-2 < PSC-3 < PSC-4 < TDM < LSC < FSC. One interface is less than another if its capability is lower, or if both are TDM and its max LSP bandwidth is lower.

Walking along an LSP path, if the interface on the near side of a link is less than the interface on the far side, the LSP has crossed a region boundary at that node, and that LSR is an edge LSR. The other edge of the region is the first later node where the capability order is reversed, as defined in the text.

Path computation may take region boundaries into account, for example by restricting a path to links whose Interface Switching Capability is PSC-1. An interface with several capabilities may or may not form a boundary, depending on which capabilities are chosen for the comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine neighbourhoods that are connected by bigger and bigger roads. When your trip moves from a small road onto a bigger one, you have crossed a border, and that is where a tunnel-road starts or ends.

sections.title: Signalling Over an FA
sections.content:
When an LSP is tunneled over an FA-LSP, the head-end of the FA-LSP treats the tail-end as adjacent, one IP hop away, when it processes the ERO in the Path or Request message. In both RSVP-TE and CR-LDP, the head-end subtracts the tunneled LSP's bandwidth from the FA's unreserved bandwidth. With link bundling it also adjusts the Max LSP bandwidth.

RSVP-TE. The Path message MUST contain an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object instead of an RSVP_HOP object, and the data interface identification MUST identify the FA-LSP. The preferred way is to send the Path message to the computed NHOP, which must be a routable address. The IP header MUST NOT have the Router Alert option, so intermediate nodes do not intercept the message, and the IP TTL versus RSVP TTL check MUST NOT be made. Instead the receiver checks that the identified data interface terminates on it, and that the PHOP is a control channel address belonging to the same node as the other end of that interface. An alternative is to encapsulate the Path message in an IP tunnel, or in the FA-LSP itself when its Interface Switching Capability is PSC-1 to PSC-4. A PathErr SHOULD contain an IF_ID HOP object, and Resv messages are IP-routed back to the PHOP and MAY be encapsulated in another IP header.

CR-LDP. The Request message MUST contain an IF_ID TLV identifying the FA-LSP, and the head-end must create a targeted LDP session with the tail-end. The Request and Mapping messages are unicast between the two.
sections.plainLanguage: When a trip goes through the tunnel-road, the starting router tells the exit router directly, you have a guest coming, and skips asking every router in between to look at the note.

sections.title: Reusing, Creating and Tearing Down FA-LSPs
sections.content:
When an LSR receives a Path or Request message, it checks whether it is at the edge of a region with respect to the ERO, using the interface switching capabilities of the previous and next hops in its IGP database. If it is, it finds the other edge of the region and extracts the ERO hops between the two edges.

It then compares those hops with the FA-LSPs it originates. If one matches, has enough unreserved bandwidth and has a compatible L3PID, the message is sent to the egress of the FA-LSP, with the FA-LSP's hops in the ERO replaced by just its end point. Otherwise the LSR sets up a new FA-LSP, which may itself cross basic TE links or other FAs, and announces it in IS-IS/OSPF as an FA. The FA's unreserved bandwidth is computed by subtracting the bandwidth of sessions pending establishment from the FA-LSP bandwidth.

The head-end may tear down an FA-LSP as a matter of local policy, and is expected to do so when no LSPs remain in it. The FA is then no longer advertised.

The holding priority of an FA-LSP is the minimum of its configured value and the holding priorities of the LSPs tunneling through it (smaller values mean higher priority). A tunneled LSP of higher priority therefore promotes the FA-LSP. When it is torn down, the FA-LSP need not drop back right away, and hysteresis may be advisable. If a holding priority is configured for an FA-LSP, this document restricts it to 0.
sections.plainLanguage: If a tunnel-road already goes where you want, you use it. If not, a new one gets built and announced. A tunnel is closed once nobody is using it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main change is that the assumption that data interfaces are bound to the interface carrying the control message is no longer valid. For RSVP, the interface a message uses may change as routing changes, so mechanisms such as security associations need a clearer definition.

The RFC points to RFC 2747, which allows an IP address as the key identifier for the sending or receiving interface. Because RSVP messages for an LSP go to an IP address identifying the next or previous hop, the text suggests replacing sending or receiving interface with the receiver's or sender's IP address. It also says the objections to IPsec AH in Section 1.2 of RFC 2747 should be revisited, since Path messages are now addressed to the receiver, not to the session destination.

CR-LDP does not have this issue because its messages run over TCP sessions that are not assumed to be between direct neighbors. The recommended mechanism for authentication and integrity of LDP message exchange is the TCP MD5 option.
sections.plainLanguage: Because letters now take a different route to reach the exit router, the old way of checking who sent each letter needs to be changed to look at the address on the envelope instead.
